newsitem.title: POLAND: BOEING OFFERS POLAND ARMS SECTOR INVESTMENT.
newsitem.headline: BOEING OFFERS POLAND ARMS SECTOR INVESTMENT.

text.p: A consortium led the Boeing Company pledged on Monday to invest heavily in Poland's arms industry if it wins a government tender to supply an avionics integration system for a planned combat helicopter.

The consortium will offer industrial schemes for several Polish arms makers worth 100 percent of the Huzar helicopter development programme, said Kenneth Medlin, general manager of Boeing's communications and combat systems division.

"We are convinced that the industrial proposals we have made for the Huzar programme are the best choice for Poland," Medlin told a news conference after a week-long tour of Polish defense aerospace and electronics firms.
The Boeing consortium also groups Sweden's Saab Dynamics, GEC-Marconi, Finmeccanica, United Technologies, Rockwell International, Orbital Science Corp. and Britain's W. Vinten.
Medlin declined to name the value of the planned investment but the consortium earlier said in a statement it estimated the costs of the Huzar development programme at $850 million.
The Polish armed forces plans to buy about 150 Huzars and Medlin said his company would embrace the helicopter and its non-military version in its worldwide marketing programme.
"There are substantial sales opportunities for... the low-cost, utility attack helicopter," Medlin said.
Sales of other equipment produced in Poland by his company and other members of the consortium would also be actively promoted, he added.
The first Huzar with the Boeing group's avionics could have its first flight in two years, Medlin later told Reuters.

The tender for the system, which would integrate the helicopter's avionics and weapon management, pits the Boeing consortium against Israel's Elbit -- a partner of the Rafael company whose NT-D anti-tank missile has been initially chosen for Huzar.

Rafael insists its NT-D missile should be integrated using Elbit-made equipment but Medlin said the demand was likely to be dropped if the Polish government chose the Israeli missile along with Boeing's avionics.
He said that while Rockwell, Boeing's partner, was offering its Hellfire II missile for the helicopter, the consortium was ready to integrate the Israeli rocket with its system.

He said that should the government drop plans to buy missiles from Israel, Rockwell could cooperate with Polish firms in manufacturing Hellfire II, its predecessor Hellfire I and possibly a next-generation missile called Brimstone.
